documents: Okuda et al. 2023, JGR Solid Earth 128, e2022JB025072, published paper (PDF, 23 pp.)

entry.evidence: experimental studies on basaltic fault rock of the type found in subduction zones, and under subduction zone conditions, are limited

steps.action: Cite seismic-reflection and geological evidence that the décollement steps down into subducting oceanic crust, with underplated basaltic layers at seismogenic-zone temperatures.
steps.quote: Such down-stepping is evident in seismic reflection data and from geological observations of underplated basaltic layers found in exhumed accretionary complexes

steps.action: Review prior friction experiments on fresh and altered basalt, chlorite and blueschist, which imply a potential for unstable friction but leave its dependence on T, Pf and effective normal stress unresolved.
steps.quote: These studies imply that subducting altered oceanic crustal material has the potential to exhibit unstable frictional behavior

steps.action: Pose the aim: characterize the frictional behavior of altered oceanic crustal material under seismogenic-zone conditions.
steps.quote: The aim was to investigate the frictional behavior of subducting oceanic crustal material under the conditions of the seismogenic zone

steps.action: Collect altered basalt from the Mugi mélange, characterize its mineralogy by microscopy, EDS and point counting, and prepare a <100 μm simulated gouge.
steps.quote: which is generally consistent with previously reported compositions of basaltic rock from the Mugi mélange

steps.action: Set laboratory conditions in a hydrothermal ring shear apparatus: T 100–550°C in 50°C stages, effective normal stress and Pf of 100 MPa, velocity steps 1–100 μm/s, with additional Pf, normal stress, low-velocity, dry and microstructural runs.
steps.quote: Laboratory friction experiments were conducted on the simulated gouge material using the hydrothermal ring shear apparatus at Utrecht University

steps.action: Estimate a universal slip-hardening trend from runs repeating the same T at different displacements, detrend μ, and derive (a−b) from local linear fits before and after each velocity step, with 95% intervals.
steps.quote: Therefore, we used 0.004 mm−1 as a universal slip-hardening trend

steps.action: Bound the detrending error by applying the 0.003 and 0.005 mm−1 trends obtained at 400°C and 250°C.
steps.quote: data may include an error in μ of ±0.05 at most

steps.action: Report μ of about 0.6 below 400°C, decreasing at low V above 400°C, and the sign of (a−b) across V-T space, defining three regimes: A and C velocity-strengthening, B velocity-weakening.
steps.quote: We define three Regimes based on the sign of (a−b) values in the V-T space

steps.action: Compare (a−b) at 250°C and 400°C from stages at different shear displacements to test for a displacement effect.
steps.quote: suggest that d has little or no systematic influence on (a−b) values at 250°C

steps.action: Check μ and (a−b) against an independent study on similar altered basalt at 150°C (Phillips et al., 2020).
steps.quote: lending support to our results and detrending strategy

steps.action: Vary pore pressure (50–200 MPa) and effective normal stress (30–100 MPa) independently at 200°C and 500°C.
steps.quote: At temperature (T) = 200°C, the (a−b) values are generally insensitive to effective normal stress

steps.action: Extend velocity steps down to 0.003 μm/s, close to the plate convergence rate, at 400°C.
steps.quote: The (a−b) values were basically negative at all tested V conditions

steps.action: Run a vacuum-dry control at 100–200°C and compare it with the wet run u968.
steps.quote: Under vacuum dry conditions at T = 100–200°C (u1003), the detrended μ values ranged from 0.59 to 0.67

steps.action: Design three constant-velocity or single-step microstructural experiments with conditions chosen inside Regimes A, B and C.
steps.quote: The temperature (T) and velocity (V) conditions of the microstructural characterization experiments were selected on the basis of the three observed Regimes

steps.action: Observe shear-band width, porosity and grain textures by SEM: porous cataclastic bands in A, denser bands with interlocking albite in B and C, and clinopyroxene indenting albite in C.
steps.quote: Albite grains in the shear band are tightly interlocked and individual grains are difficult to distinguish.

steps.action: Check by EDS, against the intact sample, that no mineral transformation occurred during the experiments, even at 550°C.
steps.quote: the mineral transformation from clinopyroxene into epidote and quartz did not happen to any detectable extent during the duration of our experiments

steps.action: Adopt the microphysical CNS model (competition between pressure-solution compaction and dilatant granular flow) as the explanatory framework, noting that it conflicts with RSF assumptions.
steps.quote: namely the Chen-Niemeijer-Spiers (CNS) model

steps.action: State the model's expectations: viscous strengthening at low V or high T, velocity weakening at balance, and higher shear-band porosity in Regime A than in B and C.
steps.quote: The model for the regime transitions predicts higher shear band porosity in Regime A and lower porosity in Regimes B and C

steps.action: Compare the model expectations with the microstructures and with the dry-versus-wet contrast in (a−b).
steps.quote: [...] clearly seen in our microstructural observations

steps.action: Retain the interpretation that pressure-solution creep of albite, competing with granular flow of clinopyroxene, produces the three-regime behavior.
steps.quote: Our interpretation is that pressure-solution creep of albite accommodates the ductile-compaction behavior

steps.action: Restrict application of the results to T < 300°C, because the natural assemblage breaks down above that temperature.
steps.quote: our experimental results and extrapolation supported by the microphysical model can only be applied to subduction depth ranges where T < 300°C

steps.action: Compare μ and (a−b) depth profiles with fresh basalt, chlorite, plagioclase/pyroxene, illite-rich shale and granite gouges from the literature.
steps.quote: Compared to fresh oceanic basalt (Zhang et al., 2017), the present altered basalt showed slightly lower μ

steps.action: Compute shear-stress depth profiles assuming λ = 0.8 and intersect them with quartz ductile strength and with field estimates from Tulley et al. (2020).
steps.quote: the altered oceanic crust have 70–90 MPa of shear stress at the depth of T = 300–400°C

steps.action: Compare (a−b) of altered basalt with sedimentary and granitic gouges below 300°C and infer a greater nucleation potential.
steps.quote: Therefore, altered basalt may be more prone to nucleating earthquakes than sediment throughout much of the seismogenic zone.

steps.action: Calculate the pore-pressure ratio needed for altered crust to be weaker than sediment, and use nucleation-size theory to argue that over-pressured crust may slip slowly.
steps.quote: the pore pressure ratio (λ) for the altered oceanic crust should be 0.88 to 0.83

steps.action: Conclude that velocity weakening of altered basalt over a wide T range implies that megathrust earthquakes could nucleate within oceanic crust at seismogenic depths.
steps.quote: suggest that megathrust earthquakes could nucleate within the oceanic crust at seismogenic zone depths

Yes; detrending bounds, displacement, Pf and normal stress, low velocity, dry control, EDS check
Kept: three-regime regularity; mechanism as best explanation

end.claim: Altered basalt gouge is velocity-weakening (Regime B) over roughly 100–450°C at 1–100 μm/s, over a wider temperature range than sedimentary gouges, so megathrust earthquakes could nucleate within altered oceanic crust at seismogenic depths (applicability limited to T < 300°C).

decisive_move.sentence: The hydrothermal ring-shear experiments, stepping T and V under controlled Pf and effective normal stress, produced the (a−b) map on which the claim rests.

gates.evidence: The main data acquisition followed a stated aim rather than a hypothesis (p. 2); only the microstructural runs were chosen to test the regimes (p. 10). The sign of (a−b) could have come out positive, and the mechanism faced the dry control and porosity predictions, but those predictions came from a model adopted after the regimes were seen (pp. 14-16). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: Scanning electron microscopy (BSE) with energy-dispersive spectrometry
Pressure-solution creep (dissolution-precipitation) as a deformation mechanism
Coulomb frictional strength combined with flow laws for strength profiles

novelty_claims.quote: we focused on altered basalt, which is a rock of subducting oceanic crust and has not been focused on as much as sedimentary rocks
Altered basalt with chlorite has only been tested under hydrothermal conditions at T = 150°C

limits: Headline status regularity_in_range covers the three-regime (a−b) map. Sub-claims: (1) the pressure-solution-of-albite mechanism is best_explanation, supported by microstructures and the dry control but with no stated rival mechanism tested; (2) earthquake nucleation in oceanic crust is best_explanation or speculative extrapolation; (3) the shear-stress and pore-pressure profiles (λ = 0.8) are calculations on assumed parameters, not tested. The slip-hardening trend is assumed to be independent of pressure and velocity. One sample from one outcrop was tested. Results above 300°C are not applicable to nature. Inference: the comparison with Phillips et al. (2020) is coded as a replication performed here, because the authors make the comparison, but the data are another group's. A composition of none_fits was chosen because the walk is a systematic laboratory parameter sweep with conditions set, followed by a post hoc mechanism drawn from a cited model; it is neither strong inference nor nature's repetition. The acknowledgments mention two anonymous reviewers, but no review file was supplied, so changes forced by review are unknown.

disagreements.support: Altered basalt shows velocity weakening over a wider T range and lower (a−b) than sedimentary gouges below 300°C.
disagreements.quote: subducting oceanic crust forms an additional or perhaps even preferred candidate for sourcing megathrust earthquakes in subduction zones

disagreements.target: Okamoto et al. (2019) on chlorite and He et al. (2013) on single-phase pyroxene and plagioclase
disagreements.support: The altered basalt assemblage is velocity-weakening over a wider T range than the single minerals, which the authors attribute to fine alteration-derived albite.
disagreements.quote: Our finding of a potential for frictional instability over a wide T range also differs from findings for chlorite

disagreements.support: The V and T dependence of (a−b) in their data conflicts with the RSF assumptions but fits the microphysical CNS model.
disagreements.quote: a V dependence of (a−b) undermines (is inconsistent with) the assumptions of the RSF formulation

disagreements.quote: do not influence the (a−b) value of altered basalt at T = 200°C unlike blueschist, actinolite-chlorite mixture, and other materials
